hypothesis: If Tertiary extinctions were gradual and place-by-place rather than catastrophic, the last occurrences of extinct genera should be spread across many Tertiary stages rather than concentrated in one or two, and genera recorded on several continents should usually disappear from those continents at demonstrably different times, more often than genera killed in the known K-Pg catastrophe.
pass_criterion: Two groups are analysed separately with Paleobiology Database genus-level occurrences from the Campanian through the Pliocene: Mollusca and Mammalia. Clause A (no catastrophic concentration): among PBDB-extinct genera whose global last occurrence (midpoint of its age range) falls in the Tertiary (Danian to Piacenzian, 17 ICS stages), the single stage holding the most last occurrences holds < 1/3 of them, and at least 4 stages are needed to accumulate 50% of them when stages are ranked by count. Clause B (place by place): among those Tertiary-extinct genera that have >= 2 occurrences on each of >= 2 continents (PBDB continent codes), the fraction whose regional last occurrences are staggered (the earliest-vanishing continent's last-occurrence minimum age is older than the last-vanishing continent's last-occurrence maximum age, i.e. non-overlapping age ranges) is > 0.5 AND exceeds the same fraction computed for the K-Pg control set (PBDB-extinct genera whose global last occurrence midpoint falls in the Maastrichtian, using Campanian-Maastrichtian occurrences). A clause passes only if it passes in both groups. Verdict 'supports' if both clauses pass, 'mixed' if exactly one passes, 'refutes' if neither passes.
fail_criterion: Clause A fails if, in either group, one Tertiary stage holds >= 1/3 of the genus last occurrences or <= 3 stages hold 50% of them. Clause B fails if, in either group, the staggered fraction is <= 0.5 or does not exceed the K-Pg control's staggered fraction (which would mean the apparent staggering is no greater than what incomplete sampling produces in a known simultaneous extinction). Both clauses failing refutes the claim; the K-Pg control itself is outside the claim's Tertiary scope and is used only as a sampling-artefact baseline.
interpretation: Darwin's 'species and groups of species' are tested at the genus level because genus-level identifications are far more complete and less affected by taxonomic noise in PBDB. 'Disappearing from one spot, then another' is read as non-overlapping last-occurrence age ranges on different continents (modern continents, PBDB cc codes). 'Swept away together by catastrophes' is read as a strong concentration of last occurrences in one or two stages. The Signor-Lipps effect makes any extinction look gradual and staggered in an incomplete record; the Maastrichtian (K-Pg) control set provides an empirical baseline for how staggered a real catastrophe looks in the same database, so clause B requires Tertiary staggering to exceed that baseline. Scope is the Tertiary, as Darwin stated; the K-Pg event itself is not used to judge the claim.
